meta.title: Who really said "Any field that has the word science in its name is guaranteed thereby not to be a science"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Feynman. Quote Investigator credits mathematician Frank Harary; the earliest documented wording is Gerald Weinberg’s 1975 systems-thinking textbook.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Any field that has the word science in its name is guaranteed thereby not to be a science'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator credits Frank Harary, documented in 1975. The earliest Feynman attribution appeared in 2008, two decades after his death.

answer.label: Not Richard Feynman — actually Frank Harary
answer.authorDates: 1921–2005 · American mathematician · a founder of modern graph theory
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Feynman said this. Quote Investigator ↗ credits the remark to Frank Harary, the graph theorist, and the earliest documented appearance it located is in Gerald M. Weinberg’s textbook An Introduction to General Systems Thinking (John Wiley & Sons, 1975), chapter 1, pages 24–25, where Weinberg reports that “Frank Harary once suggested” the law. QI is careful to call its own chronology provisional and says the 1975 citation may yet be antedated.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: An Introduction to General Systems Thinking
Gerald M. Weinberg · John Wiley & Sons, 1975 · ch. 1, pp. 24–25

source.excerpt: The misnaming of fields of study is so common as to lead to what might be general systems laws. For example, Frank Harary once suggested the law that any field that had the word “science” in its name was guaranteed thereby not to be a science. He would cite as examples Military Science, Library Science, Political Science, Homemaking Science, Social Science, and Computer Science.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ concludes: “based on current evidence the mathematician Frank Harary can be credited with this quip.” It also states plainly that its data “is not presented as definitive” and that the 1975 citation may be antedated — we have not asserted more certainty than that.

The earliest printed link to Feynman that QI found is a 2008 conference panel remark, and it quotes a different sentence: “Any field which has to have ‘science’ in its name isn’t one.” Feynman died in 1988.
The line is absent from the sourced quotations on Feynman’s Wikiquote page ↗, and QI’s Feynman tag ↗ collects a long run of similar science-flavoured lines pinned on him.
Frank Harary’s dates and field are confirmed on his Wikipedia entry ↗; Gerald M. Weinberg and the 1975 book are confirmed on his ↗.
source.excerptNote: Note the tense. Weinberg is reporting something Harary had said on an earlier occasion — “once suggested” — so even this 1975 passage does not record Harary’s own words directly. The crisp present-tense sentence in circulation is a later tidying of Weinberg’s reported version.
source.rightsHolder: John Wiley & Sons (publisher of the 1975 Weinberg text in which the remark is documented)
source.rightsNote: The only documented wording sits inside Gerald M. Weinberg’s An Introduction to General Systems Thinking, published by John Wiley & Sons in 1975 and therefore in copyright in the United States. Harary’s original spoken remark is undated and was never separately published, so nothing here can be treated as public domain.

author.name: Frank Harary
author.heading: About Frank Harary
author.bio: Frank Harary (1921–2005) was an American mathematician and one of the people who turned graph theory into a modern discipline, publishing prolifically and collaborating with an unusually large number of co-authors. He spent much of his career at the University of Michigan. The quip attributed to him here fits a mathematician’s habit of mind: it is stated as a law, and then immediately supplied with the counter-examples that test it.

misattribution.heading: How Feynman’s name got attached
misattribution.intro: This is a joke with several fathers and no birth certificate. Feynman is simply the most famous name it has drifted onto.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found no support for the attribution. Feynman died in 1988; the earliest printed linkage to him that QI located is from 2008.

QI’s earliest Feynman citation is a panel discussion printed in the Journal of Computing Sciences in Colleges in May 2008, where a speaker paraphrases: “If Richard Feynman is correct that ‘Any field which has to have ‘science’ in its name isn’t one’…” — a hedged second-hand quotation, not a source.

items.who: Max Goldstein, and an unnamed friend
items.why: The computer scientist Paul W. Abrahams credited the line to Max Goldstein of NYU in a 2007 oral-history interview, and in 1979 Marshall C. Yovits ascribed a version to “a friend”. Both are recorded by QI ↗, and both suggest a saying that spread by word of mouth among scientists rather than from one printed origin.

misattribution.truthLine: Best current evidence points to Frank Harary, reported by Gerald M. Weinberg in 1975 — not to Richard Feynman. See Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The joke works because it is a testable-sounding claim about naming, and the examples do most of the arguing: Military Science, Library Science, Political Science, Domestic Science. Weinberg presented it in 1975 not as a punchline but as an exercise — the seventh in a chapter of questions for further research — which is a rather good sign that he expected students to push back on it.

It attaches to Feynman for the same reason a hundred other sceptical one-liners do: he was a Nobel physicist with a public reputation for irreverence about pretension, and the line sounds exactly like something he would enjoy saying. Sounding right is not evidence.
context.pull: The examples do most of the arguing. That is what makes it quotable, and what makes it hard to trace.
